newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian troops to help Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: Australian troops to help Aborigines.

text.p: Australia said on Friday it would send troops into outback aboriginal villages to provide water and basic services for the country's most deprived people.
Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron said a 12-year, A$12-billion (US$9.5-billion) government spending offensive had failed to ease the suffering of most indigenous Australians.

Herron, whose government has been attacked for its handling of aboriginal affairs, pledged to abandon the "unattainable promises and exaggerated rhetoric" of the past and focus instead on "practical, common sense policies".
But he did not give details, beyond the planned pilot programme involving the army.

"I took the decision that the only way forward was to break with past practices, which clearly had not sufficiently benefited the vast majority of indigenous Australians, and instead, to pursue a direction which involved specific, measurable, and importantly, achievable outcomes," Herron said in a speech.

An aboriginal leader rejected the use of troops as a political stunt and said the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission, the main body representing indigenous minorities, had not been consulted.
"It's a political stunt," outgoing commission chief Lois O'Donoghue told reporters.
"It's a white fella's solution to an Aboriginal situation," said O'Donoghue.

In addition to sending troops into remote areas, Herron said the government would give higher priority to remote communities and was considering a programme for successful aboriginal business people to act as mentors for fellow Aborigines aspiring to establish their own business.

Aborigines, who make up less than two percent of Australia's 18 million people, have a shorter life expectancy than other Australians and often live in appalling Third World-style conditions in what is one of the region's richest countries.
"Often, I find myself asking why, in 1996, infant mortality in the aboriginal population is two to three times that of non-aboriginal Australians?" Herron said.
"(Why) life expectancy for indigenous Australians is 16 to 19 years less than for the rest of the population?
"We should never lose sight of the suffering and the downright despair, not to mention the massive waste of human talent, that such statistics represent."
Herron said the army would work with aboriginal organisations to provide water, sewerage and other essential services to isolated communities in the harsh outback.
The army would design project management and operate pilot projects that would form a model for future projects involving civilian contractors, Herron said.
The Australian army conducted a civil aid programme for remote villages in parts of the former Australian territory of Papua New Guinea before it become independendent in 1975.
The conservative Liberal-National government, which ended 13 years of Labor rule in March, has been accused by aboriginal leaders of abandoning Aborigines and widening the country's racial divide.
